title: Bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
summary: One question decides the architecture: can the model do its work before the query arrives? A bi-encoder can, so it scales. A cross-encoder cannot, so it costs a model pass per document and can only reorder a shortlist. Measured on this course's lessons, BM25 alone gets the right lesson first 30 percent of the time but has it in the top five 90 percent of the time.
html:
Phase 3 starts here, and it is the part of the course you can use at work next week. Less index internals, more decisions that change how good your answers are.

Today is the biggest of those decisions, and it reduces to one question. Can the model do its work before the query arrives?

Two ways to score a document

A bi-encoder reads the document on its own and turns it into a vector. Separately, it reads the query on its own and turns that into a vector. Then you compare the two vectors. Everything dense from days 9 to 36 works this way.

The important consequence: the document's vector does not depend on the query. So you compute it once, at ingest time, and store it. By the time a query shows up, all the expensive work on your corpus is already done.

A cross-encoder reads the query and the document together, glued into one piece of text, and outputs a single number for how relevant that document is to that query. There is no document vector. There is nothing to precompute and nothing to store, because the model's work depends on the pair. It can only happen after the query exists.

Why the cross-encoder is better

Because the words can see each other.

A bi-encoder has to compress a document into 384 numbers without knowing what will be asked about it. It is guessing at every possible question in advance. A cross-encoder already knows the question, so it can go looking for the specific thing you asked.

The cleanest place this shows up is negation. Take two documents:

A  "the rate rose in March"
B  "the rate did not rise in March"

As text those are nearly identical, and a bi-encoder pushes them to nearly the same point in space. Ask "did the rate go up" and it cannot reliably separate them, because the one word that matters got averaged in with everything else. A cross-encoder sees "up" in the query and "not" in the document at the same time and can act on it.

The analogy: a bi-encoder is writing a one paragraph abstract of every document in the archive in advance, then answering every future question by reading only abstracts. A cross-encoder is handing somebody the question and the full document and asking them to read it with the question in mind. The second is obviously better. You just cannot do it a million times.

The cost, which is not a small factor

Say you have a million documents and a query arrives.

With a bi-encoder: one model pass to encode the query, then compare that vector against a million stored vectors, which a graph index turns into roughly a thousand cheap comparisons. One model pass per query, total.

With a cross-encoder: one model pass per document, so a million model passes. A small cross-encoder on one GPU does roughly a thousand pairs a second, which puts a single query at about a thousand seconds. Call it seventeen minutes. That figure is a round order of magnitude rather than a measurement, but it is the right order of magnitude, and no amount of tuning closes a gap of a million to one.

So the cross-encoder is not a more expensive option. It is not an option at all, for search.

What you actually do

Use the bi-encoder to get from a million candidates to fifty. Then run the cross-encoder on those fifty. Fifty model passes is about fifty milliseconds, which fits in a budget.

That is the whole idea of a cascade, and it only works if the cheap stage puts the right answer somewhere in the fifty. Which is a measurable property, not a hope.

If you want to see it measured

I labelled ten questions with the lesson that actually answers each one, then ran BM25 over the 36 published lessons and recorded where the correct lesson landed.

ranks of the correct lesson:  1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 11

recall@1    3 of 10    30%
recall@3    6 of 10    60%
recall@5    9 of 10    90%
recall@11  10 of 10   100%

Read the first and third rows together, because that is the entire argument for reranking. The cheap stage puts the right answer first only 30 percent of the time, and puts it somewhere in the top five 90 percent of the time. A reranker that orders five candidates correctly turns 30 percent into 90 percent without touching the retriever.

Caveats, and they are real. Ten queries is not a benchmark, 36 documents makes a top five shortlist much easier than it would be over a million, and I wrote both the questions and the labels, which is the most common way to accidentally flatter your own system. Day 58 is about building a golden set that does not have this problem. The number to take from this is not 90 percent, it is the method: label some queries, measure how deep the right answer sits, size your shortlist from that.

One thing people get wrong

You cannot build an index out of a cross-encoder. There is no document vector to index, so there is nothing to search. A cross-encoder can only reorder a list that something else produced. If someone proposes replacing your retriever with a cross-encoder, that sentence does not have a meaning.

If you remember one thing
A bi-encoder encodes documents before the query exists, so it scales and it is vague. A cross-encoder sees query and document together, so it is accurate and costs one model pass per document. You use the first to shortlist and the second to reorder.

Tomorrow: reranking in practice, which is this idea turned into a component, and the single highest leverage upgrade available to most RAG systems.
exercise:
One. Write your day 37 note. Phase 3 starts today, so tell me whether the pitch is landing better than phase 2 did.

Two. Work out your own shortlist budget. Pick a latency figure you would accept for retrieval, say 200 milliseconds. At roughly one millisecond per query and document pair, how many candidates can a cross-encoder rerank inside it? Now halve your budget and do it again. The answer is the number that every other decision in a cascade gets built around.
